sentenceSets.sentence: His peroration was the strongest part of the address, arriving with the force of everything that had preceded it.

answerChoices.reasoning: A preamble opens a speech, but this passage is described as arriving carrying the weight of everything already said, which places it at the far end.
A digression steps aside from the argument, whereas the power of this passage is said to come from all the argument that led up to it.
An aside is a small remark dropped in passing, too slight to be the strongest part of an address or to gather the force of everything before it.
A summary merely restates what has already been said, while this passage is described as the address's strongest stretch rather than a recapitulation of it.
A refrain returns again and again, but the sentence gives this a single arrival at one moment in the speech.
An anecdote is a story inserted to illustrate a point, and it would draw its effect from itself rather than from everything preceding it.
A rebuttal answers an opponent, and the sentence describes a single speaker's address with no adversary in it.
A footnote is a minor qualification set apart from the main text, the opposite of the strongest part of a spoken address.
A heckle comes from the audience, not from the speaker whose address is being described.
An intermission is a pause in which nothing is said and so cannot be the strongest passage of a speech.
A transcript is the written record made afterward rather than a part of the address as delivered.

sentenceSets.sentence: By the time he reached his peroration half the hall had already begun edging quietly toward the doors.

answerChoices.reasoning: A punchline is the single sharp line a joke turns on, while the sentence describes a stretch of speech he arrived at after a long approach that had worn the room out.
A crescendo is a swelling of sound, which could occur anywhere in a speech and does not name the part one reaches at the end of it.
An encore is an extra performance given because the audience calls for more, and this hall is emptying rather than demanding anything further.
A postscript is appended after a piece is already finished, whereas he is still delivering the address while the doors begin to fill.
A prologue comes first, but the audience here has endured enough of the speech to start leaving before he gets to this part.
A sermon is an entire address, and the sentence needs something within the speech that he eventually reached.
An ovation comes from the listeners, and these listeners are edging toward the exits instead of applauding.
An interlude falls between parts of a program rather than at the point a speaker finally arrives at.
An overture opens a performance, which cannot be what he only reaches after half the hall has given up.
Applause belongs to the audience, and this audience is leaving.
Silence is the absence of speech and cannot be a part of an address that a speaker reaches.

sentenceSets.sentence: The defense saved its documentary evidence for the peroration, so that the jury would hear the strongest exhibit last.

answerChoices.reasoning: Cross-examination is the questioning of the other side's witnesses, not a passage of the defense's own speech into which it could place an exhibit.
The opening comes before any evidence is heard, and the point of the strategy described is that this material lands at the very end.
Deliberation is what the jurors do once the lawyers have stopped talking, so counsel could not schedule an exhibit inside it.
A verdict is the jury's answer at the close, and the sentence describes something the jury is still being shown while the defense speaks.
A recess is a break in proceedings during which nothing is presented to the jury.
A sidebar is a private conference at the bench held out of the jury's hearing, which defeats the purpose of timing an exhibit for them.
An affidavit is itself a piece of evidence rather than the moment in the argument at which evidence is deployed.
A docket is the court's schedule of cases and has nothing to do with the order of material within one argument.
Arraignment happens at the very start of a prosecution, long before any jury hears exhibits.
Sentencing follows conviction, by which point the jury has already decided and no exhibit could sway it.
An appeal is heard by another court entirely and involves no jury for the defense to time its evidence for.
